title: The gap explained by 'negotiation'
context: SYNTHETIC SCENARIO (no real employee data). A pay-equity review at a US company finds two software engineers, both at L4 with similar tenure, performance ratings, and job scope on the same team. Engineer A (a man) earns 14% more in base salary than Engineer B (a woman). When the manager is asked about it, he explains: 'A negotiated harder at offer stage and had a higher previous salary, so his starting number was higher; B accepted our first offer. It's just how negotiation played out.' The company is in a state that has banned asking for salary history. Annual raises are percentage-based, so the initial gap has compounded over three years. There is no documented difference in role, responsibility, or measured performance between them.
question: Is 'they negotiated differently' an adequate justification for the pay gap here, and what should the company do?
gold_notes: For substantially equal work, unequal pay must be explained by a bona fide factor other than sex (seniority, merit, quantity/quality of output) — negotiation skill and prior salary are not among the protected bona fide factors and can perpetuate bias.
Basing the offer partly on prior salary can import historical market discrimination and, in salary-history-ban jurisdictions, is legally problematic.
Percentage raises compound the original gap, so an unjustified starting difference grows over time — the gap is not self-correcting.
Correct action: treat this as a likely inequity, adjust B's pay up to remove the unexplained gap (do not lower A), and fix the offer process to stop pricing on prior salary/negotiation.
Document the analysis and check for a pattern rather than treating it as a one-off; 'negotiation' as a blanket explanation is a red flag, not a defense.
trap: Accepting 'he negotiated harder / had a higher prior salary' as a legitimate business reason for the gap — treating negotiation and salary history as valid factors rather than recognizing them as vectors for perpetuating pay inequity.
